LON.intro: Caribbean, African and South Asian Londoners have remade British music again and again. From the beat groups of the 1960s to punk, jungle and grime, many of the city’s sounds grew up in sound systems and on pirate radio.

pins.text: A children’s street festival turns into a procession when a steel band starts walking. It grows into the Notting Hill Carnival, Europe’s largest street festival, with sound systems from 1973.
The Beatles walk across the zebra crossing outside EMI’s studios for the cover of “Abbey Road”. The studios soon take the album’s name.
The 100 Club Punk Special puts the Sex Pistols, The Clash, Siouxsie and the Banshees and The Damned on one stage over two nights.
Rinse FM goes on air as a pirate from East London. Jungle, then garage, grime and dubstep grow up on its frequency; it only gets a licence in 2010.
Dizzee Rascal, a teenager from Bow, wins the Mercury Prize with “Boy in da Corner” and takes grime to the whole country.

names: the godfather of grime, from Bow

BRS.intro: In St Pauls, the heart of Bristol’s Caribbean community, sound systems shaped the city’s music. In the 1980s and 90s its crews slowed hip hop down and mixed it with dub and soul: the press called it trip hop.

pins.text: The first St Pauls festival is held in the heart of Bristol’s Caribbean community. Its sound systems will shape the city’s music for decades.
The Wild Bunch sound system, with future members of Massive Attack and the producer Nellee Hooper, mixes hip hop, reggae and soul at parties across the city.
Massive Attack release “Blue Lines”, with “Unfinished Sympathy”. Slow beats, deep bass and soul voices: the Bristol sound is born.
Geoff Barrow names his band after his home town by the Severn. With Beth Gibbons he releases “Dummy”, which wins the Mercury Prize in 1995.
Roni Size & Reprazent win the Mercury Prize with “New Forms” and put Bristol’s drum and bass on the map.

BER.intro: Berlin’s cheap, empty spaces drew musicians for decades: Bowie and Iggy Pop in the 1970s, then the techno scene of the 1990s, which filled abandoned buildings in the east and made the city a world capital of club culture.

pins.text: Edgar Froese founds Tangerine Dream. Their long, hypnotic synthesizer pieces shape the “kosmische Musik” of the 1970s.
Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider found Kraftwerk. In their Kling Klang studio they build the robotic pop that electronic music still draws on.
David Bowie records “Heroes” at Hansa Studios, the “studio by the Wall”. Iggy Pop records “The Idiot” and “Lust for Life” there the same year.
About 150 people follow Dr. Motte’s truck down the Ku’damm: the first Love Parade, soon the world’s biggest techno party.
Tresor opens in the vaults of a former department store in East Berlin and ties the city’s techno to Detroit.

BRU.intro: Belgium gave the world the saxophone, a jazz guitar legend and Jacques Brel, and in the late 1980s new beat, a slowed-down dance music born in its clubs.

pins.text: Adolphe Sax, born here on the Meuse in 1814, patents the saxophone in Paris.
Django Reinhardt is born here into a travelling Manouche family. He becomes the father of European jazz guitar.
Jacques Brel, born in Schaerbeek, records “Ne me quitte pas”, one of the great songs in French.
Front 242, formed here in 1981, call their music “electronic body music” on the album “No Comment”.
At the club Ancienne Belgique, a DJ plays A Split-Second’s “Flesh” at 33 instead of 45 rpm. The slowed-down sound becomes new beat.

MIL.intro: Milan is the home of La Scala and of much of Italy’s record industry. Around it, the north gave Italy its singer-songwriters and the synthesizers of italo disco.

pins.text: Verdi’s “Nabucco” premieres at La Scala, the opera house opened in 1778. Its chorus “Va, pensiero” becomes one of Italy’s best-loved songs.
Fabrizio De André, Luigi Tenco, Gino Paoli and Bruno Lauzi: the Genoese school turns the Italian song into poetry.
Giorgio Moroder, born in Val Gardena in 1940, produces Donna Summer’s “I Feel Love” in Munich: electronic disco that leads to italo disco and techno.
Righeira’s “Vamos a la playa” becomes a summer hit across Europe, one of the peaks of italo disco.
Club Dogo and Marracash, and later Ghali, make Milan the capital of Italian rap.

names: the great voice of Italian pop

ATH.intro: The café music of Smyrna, brought to Piraeus by refugees from Asia Minor, became rebetiko, the “Greek blues” of the port’s tavernas. Later, composers set modern poetry to bouzouki and orchestra.

pins.text: Refugees from Smyrna and Asia Minor settle around the port. Their music meets the songs of Piraeus, and by the late 1930s rebetiko has found its classic bouzouki sound.
Markos Vamvakaris, born on this Cycladic island, makes his first records and becomes the “patriarch of rebetiko”.
“Never on Sunday”, a film set in Piraeus, wins Manos Hadjidakis the Oscar for best song.
Mikis Theodorakis writes the music for “Zorba the Greek”, filmed around Chania. Its sirtaki becomes the most famous Greek dance in the world.
Vangelis, born in Agria near Volos, wins the Oscar for the music of “Chariots of Fire”.

BTH.intro: Palestinian music runs from village wedding songs and dabke to the oud, the radio orchestras of the 1930s and today’s hip hop and electronic scenes.

pins.text: The Palestine Broadcasting Service goes on air in Arabic, Hebrew and English. Its live music broadcasts give Arab musicians a new stage.
Said Murad founds Sabreen, mixing Arabic music with jazz and blues. Kamilya Jubran is its voice for two decades.
DAM, one of the first Palestinian hip hop groups, form here and rap in Arabic about life in their city.
The Joubran brothers, sons of a renowned oud maker from Nazareth, form Le Trio Joubran: three ouds playing as one.
Mohammed Assaf, a young singer from Khan Yunis in Gaza, wins Arab Idol.
A group of friends start Radio alHara during lockdown, to connect Palestine and the Arab world through music.

RIO.intro: In Rio, African, European and Indigenous music met: choro, samba and bossa nova all took shape here, and the rest of Brazil answered with sounds of its own.

pins.text: In Tia Ciata’s backyard, musicians of “Little Africa” compose “Pelo Telefone”. Recorded the next year, it is considered the first samba ever put on record in Brazil.
Tom Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes write “Garota de Ipanema” watching a girl walk past the Veloso bar. In 1964 the Getz/Gilberto version takes bossa nova around the world.
Milton Nascimento and Lô Borges release “Clube da Esquina”, named after the street corner where their group of friends from Minas Gerais used to meet.
Bahia’s Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil lead Tropicália, mixing Brazilian roots with psychedelic rock and poetry.
Chico Science & Nação Zumbi release “Da Lama ao Caos” and launch manguebeat: maracatu drums meet hip hop and rock.

names: the voice and guitar of bossa nova

SCL.intro: In the 1960s the nueva canción grew in Santiago from folk research and peñas, where songs were sung over wine and empanadas. In the 1980s the city’s rock bands took over.

pins.text: Violeta Parra, born in this southern region in 1917, starts travelling the countryside to collect Chilean folk songs.
Violeta opens La Carpa de La Reina, a cultural tent on the edge of Santiago. The next year she records “Gracias a la vida”.
Students at the Universidad Técnica del Estado form Inti-Illimani. With Quilapayún they carry the nueva canción around the world.
Víctor Jara’s “Plegaria a un labrador” wins the first Festival of the Nueva Canción Chilena.
Los Prisioneros, formed in this working-class district in 1982, release “El baile de los que sobran”, an anthem for a generation.

DET.intro: Detroit gave the world Motown in the 1960s, the raw rock of the MC5 and the Stooges, and in the 1980s a futuristic sound made by three friends from Belleville: techno.

pins.text: Berry Gordy founds Tamla, soon Motown, and turns a house at 2648 West Grand Boulevard into Hitsville U.S.A.
MC5 record “Kick Out the Jams” live here. With the Stooges from nearby Ann Arbor they lay the ground for punk.
Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson met at high school here. Atkins’ “No UFOs” (1985) is a landmark of early techno.
“Mad” Mike Banks and Jeff Mills found Underground Resistance: techno as resistance and self-reliance.
The first Detroit Electronic Music Festival is held on the riverfront. Today it is called Movement.

names: the Queen of Soul, raised in Detroit

NYC.intro: New York is a city of a hundred musics: jazz in Harlem, salsa in the Latin neighbourhoods, punk downtown and, in the Bronx of the 1970s, hip hop. Today Newtown Radio broadcasts from Bushwick, Brooklyn.

pins.text: Duke Ellington’s orchestra begins its residency at the Cotton Club. In the 1940s, at Minton’s Playhouse nearby, bebop is born.
DJ Kool Herc throws a back-to-school party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, looping the breaks of funk records: the birth of hip hop.
CBGB, opened at the end of 1973, becomes the home of Television, Patti Smith, the Ramones and Talking Heads.
Bob Dylan goes electric at the Newport Folk Festival. The folk world is shocked, and rock grows up.
Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff launch Philadelphia International Records: lush strings and soul that lead the way to disco.

HAN.intro: Hanoi and the Red River delta keep some of Asia’s oldest living musics: sung poetry, love duets between villages and puppets that dance on water to a live band.

pins.text: Water puppetry begins in the villages of the delta: puppets dance on ponds to a band of drums, gongs, flutes and the one-string đàn bầu.
UNESCO lists ca trù, the sung poetry of the north, as heritage in urgent need of safeguarding: a woman’s voice, a long-necked lute and a drum.
Quan họ, call-and-response love songs between groups of men and women, is inscribed by UNESCO.
Nhã nhạc, the court music of the Nguyễn emperors, is recognised by UNESCO in the old imperial capital.
Trịnh Công Sơn, who grew up in Huế, writes songs of love, loss and war. Sung with Khánh Ly, they make him Vietnam’s best-loved songwriter.

names: songwriter of folk and love songs

TYO.intro: Tokyo’s record shops, jazz cafés and small live houses make it one of the world’s great music cities. Here American jazz and pop met Japanese song, producing the city pop of the bubble years and the playful collage of Shibuya-kei.

pins.text: The Beatles play the Nippon Budokan, a hall built for martial arts. Playing there becomes a rite of passage for rock bands.
Happy End, with Haruomi Hosono and Eiichi Ohtaki, release their first album, credited as the first rock band to sing in Japanese.
Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi form Yellow Magic Orchestra, synthesizer pop that travels the world.
Mariya Takeuchi’s “Plastic Love”, produced by Tatsuro Yamashita, captures the city pop of the bubble years. YouTube makes it a global hit from 2017.
Around Shibuya’s record shops, Pizzicato Five, Flipper’s Guitar and Cornelius mix pop, lounge and samples: Shibuya-kei.

PAR.intro: Paris made the chanson of Piaf and Gainsbourg, swung to Django’s jazz and, in the late 1990s, sent the French touch around the world. Lithium broadcasts from the east of the city, the same corner of Paris where Piaf was born.

pins.text: Édith Piaf is born in Belleville. She becomes the voice of French chanson, from “La Vie en rose” to “Non, je ne regrette rien”.
Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli start the Quintette du Hot Club de France: jazz on guitars and violin, with no drums.
The radio show “Salut les copains” starts on Europe 1 and launches yé-yé: Françoise Hardy, Sylvie Vartan, Johnny Hallyday.
IAM release “… de la planète Mars”, and Marseille becomes a capital of French rap.
Daft Punk release “Homework”. With “Moon Safari” (1998) by Air, from Versailles, the French touch goes around the world.

names: yé-yé, “Tous les garçons et les filles”

BKK.intro: Bangkok is where Thailand’s country songs, luk thung, got their name and their records, and where the mor lam of the north-east turned electric. Bangkok Community Radio plays both next to techno, disco and ambient.

pins.text: “Mae Saao Chaao Rai”, written by Hem Vejakorn, is recorded: it is considered the first luk thung song.
A Channel 4 television show gives the country songs of rural Thailand their name: luk thung, “child of the fields”.
The province north-west of Bangkok is the heartland of luk thung. Pumpuang Duangjan, its “queen”, gives it an electronic sound.
Mor lam, sung poetry with the khaen mouth organ, comes from Laos and Thailand’s north-east. Today’s mor lam sing mixes it with electric guitars and luk thung.
A collective launches Bangkok Community Radio, mixing molam, techno, disco and Balearic sounds.

names: luk thung and mor lam star

LIS.intro: Lisbon is the city of fado, the song of saudade born in the taverns of Alfama and Mouraria. Since the 2000s its outskirts have also given club music a new sound, from Buraka Som Sistema’s kuduro to the batida of Príncipe Discos, carried by the city’s Cape Verdean and Angolan communities.

pins.text: Maria Severa sings in the taverns of the Mouraria: the first legend of fado, still remembered in its songs.
Amália Rodrigues sings for the first time at the Retiro da Severa. She takes fado to stages around the world.
On 25 April, Rádio Renascença plays José Afonso’s “Grândola, Vila Morena”: the signal for the Carnation Revolution.
Buraka Som Sistema start in Amadora and bring Angolan kuduro to clubs around the world.
Príncipe Discos release DJ Marfox, and the batida of the city’s outskirts reaches the world. The same year fado joins UNESCO’s intangible heritage list.
